source.title: Beyond Model Size: Probing the Gaps in Visual in-Context Learning by Training a Tiny Model
source.authors: S. Khatri; S. Landgraf; M. Ulrich; Simon Reiß

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates visual in-context learning systems across task and data shifts and argues, based on its results, that increasing model size alone does not ensure better adaptation. This bears on V6's downstream-performance-with-scale version, but it does not test language-model cross-entropy scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling-law work and compares visual in-context learning systems of different sizes on downstream visual tasks. It does not sweep model size, tokens, or compute under a controlled training setup; fit power laws; report held-out pretraining cross-entropy; or measure extrapolation. It therefore does not test V1–V5 or V7. For V6, selected primary task metrics are recorded; the paper reports additional metrics in the same tables, noted under rows_left_out.
record.test_reason: The paper compares a 1M-parameter visual in-context model with existing 300M–7B visual in-context models on image tasks. These systems differ in architecture, codebook use, training data and task exposure. There is no scale sweep, no loss curve, no power-law fit and no language model. V6 concerns downstream predictability with scale for the claim's systems, which are LM pretraining runs; the other-modality extension (V5) is about power-law loss form, which is not measured. The authors' statement that 'model size alone does not lead to improved adaptation' rests on confounded cross-system comparisons, so it is recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling model size (and data) alone does not overcome VICL's reliance on superficial routing to learned pretraining tasks. More data mainly raises the chance that a training task matches a new one. Their emphasis is that VICL benchmarking is flawed: task encodings, pretraining-task overlap and pixel-wise metrics misrepresent contextual adaptation. They call for context-sensitive metrics and architectural or data-distributional methods.
record.recipe_differences: No language-model scaling-law experiment, loss-curve fitting, compute sweep, or matched model-size training series; evaluates existing visual in-context learners and a separately trained 1M-parameter visual model on task benchmarks.
record.method_sensitivity: Task encoding changes outcomes; the paper reports substantially different depth RMSE when the depth-map encoding changes. Image/task distribution and prior exposure to a task also vary across evaluations.

fits_no_version.finding: Across unmatched visual in-context learners (1M U-Net vs 300M/1B DeLVM, 7B LVM, MAE-VQGAN), parameter count does not order performance. TinyVICL is best on DID-MDN de-raining (LPIPS 0.1247 vs 0.1579–0.5434), BSDS500 edge F1 (0.31 vs ≤0.0752) and colorization metrics. LVM and MAE-VQGAN are best on PASCAL segmentation. DeLVM 1B vs 300M differ little. Results depend heavily on task encoding and on metric choice.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In visual in-context learning, downstream adaptation across heterogeneous systems is driven more by task encoding, pretraining-task overlap and output representation than by parameter count.

record.problems: The model comparisons are not controlled scaling experiments: systems differ in architecture, training data, task exposure, and output representation. The paper reports no uncertainty estimates and no held-out pretraining cross-entropy or scaling-law fits. Several quantitative metrics are discussed as imperfect proxies for contextual task performance.
record.rows_left_out: For Tables 1–5, omitted other reported metrics for conditions already represented by a selected primary metric, including additional de-raining, edge-detection, segmentation, depth, and colorization measures. Also omitted Table 2 Copy Context control rows and Table 5 Copy Context colorization row. These tables report those results separately; they were left out to stay within 60 rows and because they do not change the selected-metric pattern.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No loss-scaling curves for vision models; only task metrics of unmatched systems.
No controlled scale series or loss-to-downstream relation. Only unmatched systems differing in architecture, data and task exposure.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

record.verdict_notes: Reclassified from tests/T5 to discusses/T6. The size comparison confounds architecture, codebook, training data and task exposure. The authors themselves attribute much of the gap to codebooks and encoding mismatch, not scale. Rows r58/r59 duplicate r36/r38. Rows r46/r47 duplicate r35/r31. Text-only result: LVM edge F1 rises from 0.0752 to 0.2296 with its training encoding.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute; bottleneck conditions; several-orders-of-magnitude power-law behavior.
Fitting laws on smaller runs and testing predictions on larger runs.
Compute-budget sweeps and loss-minimizing parameter/token allocations.
Controlled comparisons of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Testing whether power-law loss curves hold in vision or other training regimes; the paper evaluates visual task performance, not loss scaling curves.
No pretraining-loss-to-downstream-performance relationship or controlled scale sweep; visual systems differ in architecture, training data, and task exposure.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or scaling-curve bends.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: DID-MDN de-raining, BSDS500 edge detection, and ImageNet colorization; comparisons with larger listed VICL models
reader_labels.reason: TinyVICL scores better than the larger listed models on the selected metrics for these settings, so the reported downstream outcomes do not show a consistent improvement with model size (rows r01–r10 and r52–r56).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: PASCAL VOC segmentation, NYU depth estimation, and altered depth encodings
reader_labels.reason: Results vary by task and model: larger systems outperform TinyVICL in many segmentation and depth comparisons, but not uniformly; depth scores also change substantially with encoding. These are non-controlled cross-model comparisons, not a stable scale trend (rows r11–r35 and r46–r51).
